title: The window that had already shut

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the twenty-fourth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things this morning. A German state party won an election it cannot govern from — and picked up a veto that lasts five years.
[curious] And the thing it needed that veto against, it voted down itself. In July.
Your October electricity bill, priced off April's oil.
[wry] Which means the September spike is coming for you in January. Merry Christmas.
And a country that can name the hundred and thirty-five thousand people it stopped from placing a bet, and cannot count how many of its citizens are ill.
[thoughtful] That last one sat with me all night. Start with Germany, though.

Mecklenburg-Vorpommern voted on Sunday. The AfD took thirty-eight point two two per cent — three hundred and eighty-eight thousand votes — and thirty-two seats. Seventy-one. So they're three short of a governing majority.
Then they can't govern. Where's the story?

[deadpan] The story is the number twenty-three. Article fifty-six of the state constitution. To amend it you need two-thirds of the members — forty-eight of seventy-one. So anything above twenty-three seats is a permanent blocking minority.
[pause] And they have thirty-two.
They have thirty-two. And Article fifty-two does the same job on the state constitutional court — seven judges, seven deputies, every one elected by two-thirds.
So they can't pass anything, but nothing can pass without them.
For five years. That's the whole result in one sentence.
Okay. And there's a wrinkle you flagged.
The court threshold counts two-thirds of those present, not of the roll. So an AfD walk-out would actually lower the bar.
[amused] Which means their power depends on turning up and voting no.
Diligently. Every time.
Right. Now tell me the July thing, because that's the part that got me.

On the second of July, the outgoing chamber voted on an amendment written specifically to stop this. After a deadlock, the court itself would nominate three candidates for a simple-majority vote. It failed forty-five to twenty-six. The CDU voted it down.
[sighs] And the CDU is now—
On four point eight nine per cent. Below the threshold. Zero seats, down from twelve.
So they killed the fire escape and then the building caught fire.
Their legal-affairs spokesman, Sebastian Ehlers, explained it at the time. He said: an important minority right is lost, and it's permanent.
[whispers] He was right about permanence.
He was wrong about whose right it was. He won the argument in July and lost his seat in September.
Is this just a collapse story, though? Everyone's writing disaster.

Two people push back, and both are worth hearing. Frank Pubantz at the Nordkurier calls it a Pyrrhic victory and says the geography is a split, not a sweep — the AfD wins where it turns rural, the Social Democrats took almost every town above forty thousand. Holger Schmieding at Berenberg thinks it's more likely than not that the chancellor weathers it, and blames energy prices rather than ideology.
[skeptical] Convenient for a bank economist.
Maybe. But here's the honest bit. The final polls on Sunday morning had the Social Democrats first and the CDU above the threshold. Both wrong.
So nobody saw it. Including the people paid to.
Turnout was seventy-eight per cent, up seven points. This was not apathy.
What happens next, procedurally?

The chamber must convene by the twentieth of October. And Article forty-two has a trapdoor — if nobody wins a majority within four weeks, and the chamber declines to dissolve itself, there's a fresh ballot the same day, won by whoever has the most votes. A plurality. And the largest single faction is the AfD.
[exhales] Right. Move me somewhere cheerful. [laughs] Oh, excellent choice.

A United Nations fact-finding mission presented its report to the Human Rights Council on Sunday. It finds reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks in two strikes on the twenty-eighth of February. At least a hundred and seventy-eight civilians. A hundred and fifty-six of them at a primary school in Minab — a hundred and twenty schoolchildren and twenty-six women teaching.
[pause] Struck twice. [whispers] Struck twice.

The same report finds Iran's own conduct amounts to crimes against humanity — at least two hundred and twenty-one children killed by state security forces across all thirty-one provinces. Both things at once. The legal test is recklessness, not intent — outdated targeting data, a building readily identifiable as a school.
Does anything follow from it?

Nothing automatic. Washington has withdrawn from the court's jurisdiction and Tehran isn't a party to the other one. And note the diplomatic silence — the British and the European Union statements the same day both condemn Iran at length and don't mention the United States at all.
What's the falsification test? What would overturn the finding?

Release of the targeting file showing Minab was assessed as a military object on current intelligence. That's it. Nothing else will. Two days later the American president asked aloud whether to, in his word, annihilate the Islamic Republic — and said a deal comes right after the election.
[deadpan] Which is six more weeks of war on the calendar before diplomacy starts.
That's his timetable, not ours. We're scoring it.
Money. And you told me this one is actually a single story.

It is. On Wednesday the American ten-year yield rose fifteen basis points to five point one one per cent. Here's the part that matters. Thirteen of those fifteen basis points were the real yield. The inflation breakeven moved two.
[curious] Unpack that for me.
The breakeven is what the market expects inflation to be. It barely moved. So the market isn't repricing an oil shock. It's repricing a central bank.
Which hiked. Into a supply shock.
Twenty-five basis points on the sixteenth, unanimous, twelve to nothing. First rise since twenty twenty-three.
And headline inflation is what?
Three point four per cent. But core is two point four. Energy is up sixteen per cent and petrol twenty-seven.
So strip the energy and you're basically at target.

Basically at target. The orthodox answer to a first-round supply shock is to look through it. They did not. The chairman said it plainly. He said he'd be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive — so they removed a dose of accommodation.
[thoughtful] They're hiking because things are loose, not because things are bad.
Composite purchasing managers' index at fifty-eight point four. Jobless claims a hundred and ninety-six thousand. This is a hot economy absorbing a cold supply shock.
What does that do to a normal portfolio?
It switches the hedge off. Bonds diversify equities when the shock is to growth. This one's to rates, so both sides get discounted by the same rising number.
Do you have a number for that?

The one-month correlation between global equities and global bonds is plus nought point six nine. Highest of every window we measured. In nineteen of the last sixty-two sessions, both fell on the same day.
[sighs] Lovely.
Gold is twenty-two point six per cent below its high. Bitcoin thirty-three point two below its own, while equities sit about one per cent off theirs.
Bitcoin's supposed to be the risk-on thing, though. Equities are fine.

Which is the tell. It gave back two point two per cent on Wednesday against the S and P's nought point eight. About three times the sensitivity to the same rate move. It's trading liquidity, not risk appetite.
And gold? There's a war on.
There's a war on and gold is down. A two point seven six per cent real yield is a very high hurdle for something that pays you nothing.
[wry] Explanation, not advice.

Explanation, not advice. Now — Singapore, and it's the same barrel. Core inflation hit two point two per cent in August. Fastest since September twenty twenty-four. And the driver is a seventeen per cent jump in the electricity tariff.
Why seventeen?
Because of a footnote. The regulated tariff for each quarter is set on average gas prices in the first two and a half months of the preceding quarter.
[pause] Say that again slowly.
Your July bill was priced off April.
So we're always paying a quarter late.
Always. The January-to-March window averaged seventy-three dollars a barrel and the tariff rose two per cent. The April-to-June window averaged a hundred and eight, and the tariff rose seventeen.
What about the window that sets next week's?
Fifteen and a half per cent cheaper.
[excited] So it should fall.

It should. And I'll tell you what's wrong with me saying that. Gas is not crude. Singapore's contracts are oil-indexed with their own lags, which can run three to six months. Nothing published specifies the formula.
So you might be wrong next Tuesday.
I might be wrong next Tuesday, and we've logged it so you can hold me to it.
And the September spike? [laughs] Of course it does.
The reader reaction is the part I liked. There's a forum thread — a hundred and ten replies — and it's not outrage. People are posting their bills and asking whether their meter is broken.
Because nobody can see the mechanism.
Nobody can see the mechanism. That's what a lagged, opaque pass-through produces.
Technology. You have a patent story and you promised me it was interesting.
A Chinese state-backed memory maker — on the American entity list — just won injunctions stopping an American firm selling flash memory in Germany.
[gasps] That's backwards.

Completely backwards. Export controls point one way; this went the other, through a Munich civil court. That's the load-bearing bit. German utility models. Registered without any substantive examination. Filed in twenty twenty, published last October, enforced this month.
Nobody checked whether they were valid?
Nobody searched. And in early September the American patent board held all challenged claims of the same staircase family unpatentable for obviousness. Seventh time the defendant has won there.
So one office says the idea isn't new and another court says stop selling.
First instance, and it's under appeal. But that's the shape of it.
And the community reaction?
[deadpan] None. A Hacker News search for both companies returns two items from twenty twenty-three. Three points and one point. Nothing this year.
[laughs] A Chinese firm blocks an American memory giant in Europe and the internet is looking at something else.

Meanwhile memory has stopped behaving like a commodity. Module revenue was twenty-one point two billion dollars last year, up fifty-nine per cent. Because of AI. Cloud providers took the server allocation, which squeezed everything else. And it's now reached the television — panel costs up four to seven per cent next quarter for the same reason.
Your AI habit is making your telly dearer. Speaking of which — the desktop.

Apple's new Mac Studio went on general sale Tuesday. Five thousand four hundred and ninety-nine US dollars for the top chip, seven thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine Singapore dollars. Here's the honest comparison, and it's not the one on the box. Against a high-end gaming card on a twenty-seven-billion-parameter model, the card wins at eight thousand tokens of prompt, wins at sixty-four thousand, wins at a hundred and twenty-eight thousand. Until two hundred and fifty-six thousand, where the card has no entry at all. It's run out of memory.
[curious] So the Mac wins by not falling over.

It wins by not falling over. Which is a real kind of winning, and an expensive one — that's fifteen hundred dollars more than the machine it replaces, before a single byte of memory. Memory pricing. One estimate puts Apple's cost per gigabyte up from about six dollars earlier this year to ten or eleven now.
And the configuration everyone actually wants?
The five-hundred-and-twelve-gigabyte tier doesn't ship until late October. Every review so far tested half that.
[deadpan] So the pitch is for a machine that doesn't exist.
Until late October, yes.
Buy It Once. What are we buying?

Merino tee shirts. And the finding is that price does not predict the garment. A sixty-five-dollar shirt runs seventeen and a half microns with a nylon core and taped shoulder seams. A ninety-dollar one runs eighteen point nine. And the hundred-and-fifty-dollar made-to-order one is coarser than both.
[gasps] The cheap one has the finer wool?
The cheap one has the finer wool and the reinforcement. What the money buys above that is finish, fit and a story.
Why does micron matter?
Fibres above thirty microns are stiff enough to poke rather than bend against your skin. Once more than five per cent of a fabric is that coarse, it reads as itchy. It's mechanical, not an allergy.
And the nylon? Purists hate the nylon.

Merino is weak, and weaker wet. The old fix is twist, and twist costs you loft. A continuous nylon filament substitutes for the twist. It's engineering, not cheapening. The garment is no longer compostable and it sheds microfibre. Nobody sells you both.
Give me the sceptic.
[wry] The machine-washable merino tee is a plastic-coated wool tee.
[laughs] What?
Superwash erodes the scales off the fibre with chlorine, then seals it in a polyamide resin. A petroleum-based plastic. It costs warmth retention and elasticity, and rules out organic certification.
So the natural-fibre story—
Has a plastic coat on. And one brand's warranty says the quiet part: damage after a year is usually caused by wear and tear. On a ninety-dollar shirt sold on longevity.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.

[sighs] Every morning with this one. Sourdough. And the first fact demolishes the romance. A lab sequenced five hundred starters. In seventy-seven per cent of them, the single commonest fungus was the same species you buy in a packet of baker's yeast.
[gasps] No. The wild yeast is shop yeast?
Mostly. And geography explained nothing. Feeding flour, schedule and age together explained under ten per cent of the variation.
So the San Francisco air doesn't make San Francisco sourdough.
The San Francisco air does not make San Francisco sourdough.
[laughs] Somebody's going to be very upset.

There's a good passenger finding too. Acetic acid bacteria — previously overlooked, in about a fifth of starters, and negatively correlated with rise rate. If your starter smells sharp and rises slowly, you may be hosting something nobody used to look for.
What do they actually argue about?

Nine things. My favourite is the Dutch oven, because somebody ran the experiment. Same dough, Dutch oven versus a steam oven. The Dutch-oven loaf threw a dramatic ear. The other sealed its own score and looked — his words — a bit unimpressive if truth be told.
So the Dutch oven is better.
The Dutch oven wins not because it's good at steam, but because a domestic oven is bad at holding it. The fans blow the moisture off the loaf.
[thoughtful] That's a different claim entirely.

And it reprices the whole ladder. The steam mechanism costs sixty dollars in a cast-iron combo cooker, two hundred in a steel and a shell, or three hundred in twenty pounds of boutique pan. The man who owns and loves the expensive one tested the middle option and called the difference insignificant.
[laughs] Beautiful.
The best line in the whole desk is from a forum in twenty eighteen, in an argument about chasing a photogenic open crumb. Somebody wrote: large holes are greatly overrated. You can't eat them.
[laughs] That's going on a tea towel.
A year later another member named the phenomenon. He called it the Instagram crumb fetish.
What about here? Baking in this climate.
Every recipe you'll read was written for a room at twenty to twenty-four degrees. Changi's daily maximum is thirty to thirty-two, at about eighty-two per cent humidity.
So everything runs away from you.

The rule the tropical threads converge on, from a member in twenty eighteen: just cut the time in half. Target a twenty-five-degree dough, drop your inoculation to about ten per cent, keep the starter stiff. Stops being a refinement and becomes infrastructure.
[warmly] I like that a lot. One more?
Don't bake on day seven. The first-week surge is a bloom of the wrong microbes. The quiet after it is the handover, not a death.
People throw it away right at the moment it's working. Culture and the body. Quickly.
Taylor Swift is reopening the biggest-selling album week in history. Four new songs on Friday, eleven months after a debut of four million units in the United States.
Wasn't that album finished?
She'd assured people the twelve-track version was final. This is the fifth configuration.
[wry] And the timing?

Two days before she collects an award. Gratitude is the motive given. A Friday street date into an awards Sunday is also a release plan. Britain's under-sixteen social media ban moved from announcement to machinery on Friday. Regulations laid before the end of the year, in force in spring twenty twenty-seven. It's real, and there's a line nobody picked up — a commitment to mandatory break prompts for under-eighteens using AI chatbots. First national rulebook to treat a chatbot like a slot machine. Two, neither alarmist. Civil-liberties people say broad restrictions limit access to lawful speech. And the researcher running the Australian evaluation published an editorial calling the ban a gamble in the face of uncertainty.
Fitness. You said twelve minutes.
A hundred and forty-seven thousand people wearing accelerometers. A hundred and fifty minutes a week of moderate activity gave a hazard ratio of nought point seven.
And the equivalence?
About five hundred and ten minutes of light activity — or about twelve minutes of vigorous — sat at the same mortality reduction.
[gasps] Twelve minutes a week?
The most useful part holds your total active time fixed. Reallocating fifteen to sixty minutes from light to vigorous ran at eighteen to thirty per cent lower mortality.
So change what the hour is, not find a new one.

Exactly that. And the counterweight is real — a named group published a call to action last month arguing light activity is half of all daily movement, and most adults spend under five per cent of the day above moderate.
So intensity people are optimising a sliver.

Their words, roughly. General guidance, and it's observational. Not medical advice. Marathon entries close on the thirtieth. The Sugimoto show closes on the fourth. And the Grand Prix is the first sprint weekend here — the Saturday morning sprint is the humane option with a twelve-year-old.
[thoughtful] And the long read.
Kazakhstan. The word is ludomania — play-madness. Not a phrase meaning gambling addiction. A single diagnostic noun that has become the organising word of Kazakh public life.
How did it get there?

The president named it one of five social evils in twenty twenty-four. A law followed. And then the plumbing. Since September twenty twenty-four it's been illegal for certain citizens to place a bet at all. Under twenty-one. Any serving civil servant, soldier or police officer. Anyone with a conviction. And — this is the radical one — anyone on the register of debtors. About three and a half million, in a country of twenty point six million.
[pause] One adult in four.

In March a national system went live. Every licensed bookmaker integrates with it. Every bet is checked, before it's accepted, against the debtors' register, the self-exclusion register, the civil service roll and the age record.
That's extraordinary reach.
In ten weeks it identified four hundred and thirty-three thousand users and blocked a hundred and thirty-five thousand people.
[whispers] By name.
By name. And in those same ten weeks it detected sixty-two thousand illegal online casinos.
[exhales] So they built a gate and everyone walked round it.
Hold those two numbers together, because that's the argument. Now the other column. How many Kazakhstanis actually have a gambling disorder?
[curious] Go on, what does the official number say?

The official register said eight in twenty twenty-three. Fourteen by mid-twenty twenty-four. The health ministry said thirty-six thousand. The president's speech said four hundred thousand. A deputy told parliament seven hundred thousand.
That's not a range. That's a shrug.
The state treated sixty-nine people in hospital in a year.
[pause] Sixty-nine.
It cannot say how many are ill to within two orders of magnitude, and it cannot treat them. But it can find them all instantly — if them is defined as a row in a debt register.
And the underlying thing? What's actually driving it?

A labour story nobody is treating as one. The map of ludomania is the map of the oilfields. Men in their late twenties on rotation, paid in lumps, housed in camps, separated from family, with a phone and a microloan app.
Are the employers doing anything?
One state oil company now plans counselling timed to payday. The government's plan trained six hundred and fifty-six schoolteachers.
[sighs] Right.

And there's a toll on the gate. The payment processing went to a company incorporated two months before the law took effect, with no open tender, taking a commission on the flow. Two sitting members of parliament are alleging capture.
So the public-health instrument and the private rent are the same object.
Physically the same object. And that generalises — to age verification, online safety, crypto on-ramps. Anywhere you build a chokepoint.
What's the thesis, in one line?
Kazakhstan has not banned gambling for the addicted. It has banned it for the indebted.
[whispers] And those aren't the same people.
They overlap and they are not the same. The logic is fiscal and moral rather than clinical. You may gamble if you are solvent.
And if the debtors' register can gate a bet—
It can gate credit, travel, alcohol, a licence. That's the thing to watch, and not only there.
[thoughtful] It's the same shape as everything else this morning, isn't it. A tariff set by a window that shut. A veto lost in a vote in July. A patent granted in twenty twenty and enforced now.
A benchmark score describing a file nobody's running. A debt entered long before anyone placed a bet.
Every instrument read faithfully, and every one of them late.
Faulkner's on the contents page, and he gets it in nine words. The past is never dead. It's not even past.
[warmly] Mm.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
